full_judgment:
14. In all the cited cases their Lordships held that in each and every contract entered into between the Government and a private individual writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked because the remedy lies in damages. Modern Government has multifarious activities. Some of its functions are governmental function while exercising sovereign power and again, some of the functions can be described as trading functions. When the Government after accepting the tender places an order for supplying, say, for ten thousand chairs, and the supplier agreed to do so a contract is entered into, there is offer and its acceptance backed by obligation. A full-fledged contract comes into existence. Here the Government functions in the capacity as a trader eg, an ordinary buyer; and if there is a breach of such contract the aggrieved party can sue for damages or any other appropriate remedy, but cannot invoke writ jurisdiction. However, if the contract is rooted in any statute for enforcement of the same writ jurisdiction can, of course, be invoked such as the lease of haat, bazar, fishery, khash land, etc. or if there is any international contract. Even in case of a private contract being a trading contract if the Government acts with malafide intention Writ petition for breach of obligation against the Government lies. 

 15. There cannot be any dispute about the proposition and pronouncement of the highest courts of both Bangladesh and India. From the facts and circumstances of the instant case we find that no contract has yet been entered into by the Government with any of the parties including the petitioner or, for that matter, with respondent No. 4, only the process of comparative study of the bids was assessed by the purchase committee and this is neither in exercise of sovereign power of the Government nor in respect of haat, bazar, fishery or khas land nor the contract is rooted in any statute.
